title: Caring for Your Chain
description: A clean, lubed chain shifts smoothly, lasts longer, and protects your cassette and chainring from premature wear.

sections.content: Your chain is the hardest-working part of your drivetrain — and the most neglected. A clean, lubed chain shifts smoothly, lasts longer, and protects your cassette and chainring from premature wear.

sections.heading: How Often?
sections.content: Every 100–150 miles in dry conditions, or after every wet or muddy ride. If your chain looks brown or gritty, or sounds noisy while pedaling, it's overdue.

sections.heading: What You'll Need
items: Chain degreaser
A chain cleaning tool or a rag
Chain lube (wet lube for wet conditions, dry lube for dry)
A clean rag

steps.title: Wipe off excess
steps.body: Before doing anything, wipe the chain down with a dry rag to remove loose dirt and old lube.

steps.title: Degrease
steps.body: Apply chain degreaser and work it in with a chain cleaning tool or rag. Run the chain through a few times until it runs clear.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.body: Rinse with water if using a water-soluble degreaser, then dry thoroughly with a clean rag.

steps.title: Lubricate
steps.body: Apply lube to each link while slowly backpedaling. One drop per link is enough. Run the drivetrain through all the gears to make sure lubricant makes it into every nook and cranny.

steps.title: Wipe off excess lube
steps.body: Let it sit for a minute, then wipe off any excess lube with a dry rag. Excess lube attracts dirt.

sections.heading: Signs of Wear
sections.content: Chains stretch over time. A stretched chain wears out your cassette and chainring faster. Use a chain wear indicator tool — replace your chain at 0.5–0.75% stretch to protect your drivetrain.

title: Checking and cleaning your brake pads
description: How to inspect and clean your brake pads to maintain stopping power and safety.

sections.content: Your brake pads are your first line of safety. Worn or contaminated pads reduce stopping power — sometimes dramatically — before you ever notice a problem. A quick inspection every month can protect both your bike and yourself.

sections.heading: How Often?
sections.content: Check pads every 4–6 weeks, or any time you notice reduced braking performance, squealing, or grinding. After wet or muddy rides, always give them a quick look.

sections.heading: What You'll Need
items: Isopropyl alcohol (rubbing alcohol)
Clean lint-free rags or paper towels
A flashlight or headlamp
A ruler or calliper (optional)

steps.title: Find the pads
steps.body: Look at your brake caliper — the clamp straddling the rotor (disc brakes) or rim (rim brakes). Shine a light into the caliper to see the pads on either side of the rotor or rim surface.

steps.title: Check pad thickness
steps.body: The friction material should be at least 1.5mm thick (disc brakes) or have visible material above the wear indicator line (rim brakes). If you can barely see any pad material, it's time to replace them.

steps.title: Inspect for contamination
steps.body: Look for oily residue, glazed shiny spots, or embedded debris. Oil is the main culprit — even a small amount on a rotor or rim can ruin a set of pads.

steps.title: Clean the pads
steps.body: Dampen a clean rag with isopropyl alcohol and wipe down the pad surface. Use a fresh section of rag for each swipe. Do the same to the rotor or rim. Never use soap, water, or any lubricant near brakes.

steps.title: Let dry and test
steps.body: Let air dry for a minute, then take a slow roll and squeeze the brakes firmly a few times to bed them back in.

sections.heading: Signs of Wear
items: Pad material less than 1.5mm thick (disc) or worn to the indicator line (rim)
Grinding or metallic scraping — the backing plate is contacting the rotor
Heavy oil contamination that does not improve after cleaning
Uneven or cracked pad surface

sections.content: When lubricating your chain, always cover your rotors and brake calipers first. A single overspray can contaminate pads beyond recovery.

title: Standard vs. Wax Chains: What's the Difference?
description: A straightforward breakdown of traditional chain lube vs wax — and how to know which is right for you.

sections.content: If you've spent any time in cycling circles lately, you've probably heard people talking about wax chains. But is it worth switching from the lube you've been using for years? Here's a straightforward breakdown.

sections.heading: How standard chain lube works
sections.content: Traditional chain lubes — wet, dry, or all-conditions — coat the chain's moving parts with an oil-based film. They're easy to apply, widely available, and forgiving. The downside: oil attracts dirt and grime, which turns into an abrasive paste that accelerates wear on your chain, cassette, and chainrings.

sections.heading: How wax chains work
sections.content: Wax lubrication works differently. The chain is immersed in molten paraffin wax, which bonds to the metal and dries to a hard, clean coating. Because wax is dry, it doesn't attract dirt the same way oil does. A waxed chain runs cleaner and can last significantly longer — some riders report 2–3x chain life compared to oil lube.

sections.heading: Is wax right for you?
sections.content: Wax makes the most sense for road and gravel riders who want maximum drivetrain efficiency and cleanliness. Mountain bikers can use it, but frequent wet and muddy conditions mean more frequent reapplication. If you ride in variable conditions or just want a simple low-maintenance solution, a quality wet or dry lube still does the job well.
If you're switching to wax for the first time, you need to completely degrease your chain first — or start with a fresh chain. Wax doesn't bond properly over oil residue.

title: How to Add Sealant to a Tubeless Tire
description: Tubeless sealant dries out over time. Here's how to top it up and keep your tires rolling.

sections.content: Tubeless sealant is what makes a tubeless setup work — it coats the inside of the tire and instantly plugs small punctures as you ride. But sealant dries out over time, so topping it up regularly is one of the most important things you can do to keep your tires rolling.

sections.heading: How Often?
sections.content: Every 3–6 months in normal conditions, or sooner if you notice your tire losing air faster than usual. In hot, dry climates sealant dries out faster — check every 2–3 months. After a big puncture, always top up — the sealant used to plug the hole is gone.

sections.heading: What You'll Need
items: Tubeless sealant (your preferred brand)
A sealant injector or large syringe
Tire levers (just in case)
A pump or CO2 inflator
Clean rags

steps.title: Remove the valve core
steps.body: Using a valve core tool or the back of most valve caps, unscrew the valve core and set it somewhere safe. Don't lose it.

steps.title: Check remaining sealant
steps.body: Shake the wheel. If you hear sloshing, there's still some sealant in there — you may just need a top-up. If it's silent and dry, you'll need a full refill (about 2–4oz depending on tire size).

steps.title: Inject the sealant
steps.body: Draw sealant into your injector and insert it into the valve stem. Slowly push the sealant in. For a road tire, 2oz is typical. For gravel or MTB, 3–4oz.

steps.title: Reinstall the valve core
steps.body: Screw it back in firmly but don't overtighten.

steps.title: Inflate and slosh
steps.body: Inflate to your normal riding pressure, then rotate the wheel to coat the inside of the tire evenly. Give it a few spins in each direction.

steps.title: Check for leaks
steps.body: Look around the bead and valve for any sealant seeping out. A little at the valve is normal — wipe it off and it should seal within a minute.

sections.heading: Signs It's Time
items: Tire losing air noticeably between rides
Dry, chalky residue inside the tire (no liquid left)
Sealant has chunked up and won't flow
More than 6 months since last top-up

sections.content: Always carry a small bottle of sealant on longer rides. If you get a puncture that won't seal on its own, injecting fresh sealant through the valve can often save the ride without needing a tube.

title: MTB Brake Pad Types: Resin, Metallic, and Semi-Metallic
description: The material your pads are made from affects feel, lifespan, and performance. Here's how to choose the right type for your riding.

sections.content: Not all brake pads are created equal. The material your pads are made from affects how they feel, how long they last, and how well they perform in different conditions. Here's what you need to know before your next pad swap.

sections.heading: Resin (Organic) Pads
sections.content: Resin pads are made from a mixture of organic materials bonded together — think rubber, kevlar, and other fibers. They're the most common type found stock on new bikes. Strong points: quiet and smooth with little noise or vibration, gentle on rotors, good initial bite. Weaknesses: fade under heat on long descents, wear faster than metal pads, poor wet performance. Best for: trail riders and anyone prioritizing a quiet smooth feel over raw power.

sections.heading: Metallic (Sintered) Pads
sections.content: Metallic pads are made by compressing and heating metal particles — copper, iron, and other alloys — into a dense hard compound. Strong points: heat resistant on long descents, long lasting, strong in wet and muddy conditions. Weaknesses: more prone to squealing, harder on rotors, less initial bite until warmed up. Best for: enduro and gravity riders, heavy riders, anyone doing big descents or riding in consistently wet conditions.

sections.heading: Semi-Metallic Pads
sections.content: Semi-metallic pads combine metal particles with organic binders to get the best of both worlds. Strong points: better heat resistance than resin, more initial bite than full metallic, decent in varied conditions. Weaknesses: don't fully excel in any one area, can still squeal in wet conditions. Best for: all-mountain and trail riders who want a versatile pad for varied conditions.
Mixing pad types front and rear is totally fine — many riders run metallic up front for maximum stopping power and resin in the rear for modulation and feel.

title: When to Replace Your Tires
description: Tires don't make noise when they're past their prime — they just fail. Here's how to know when it's time for new rubber.

sections.content: Tires are one of the most safety-critical parts of your bike, and also one of the easiest to neglect. Unlike a worn chain, a tire doesn't make noise when it's past its prime — it just fails when you least expect it. Here's how to know when it's time for new rubber.

sections.heading: How Often?
sections.content: Give your tires a quick visual inspection before every ride. A more thorough check every 4–6 weeks will catch problems early before they become a roadside emergency.

steps.title: Worn tread
steps.body: Most tires have small wear indicator holes or dimples in the center of the tread. When those disappear, the tire is done. No indicator? Look for the tread pattern becoming flat and smooth in the center contact patch — that's your signal.

steps.title: Cracking or dry rot
steps.body: Small cracks in the rubber, especially on the sidewalls, mean the tire compound is breaking down. This happens from age, UV exposure, and ozone — even if you haven't ridden many miles. A tire that's 3–5 years old should be replaced regardless of visible tread.

steps.title: Cuts and slices
steps.body: Small surface cuts are usually fine. Deep cuts that expose the casing beneath — the woven fabric layer — compromise the tire's structure. If you can see threads, replace the tire.

steps.title: Persistent punctures
steps.body: If a tire keeps going flat in the same spot, the casing may be damaged or the bead compromised. Even if it holds air between rides, repeated punctures in the same location are a sign the tire is done.

steps.title: Bulges or deformations
steps.body: A bulge anywhere on a tire — tread or sidewall — means the internal structure has failed. This tire can blow out without warning. Replace it immediately.

steps.title: Sidewall damage
steps.body: The sidewall is thinner and more vulnerable than the tread. Cuts, tears, or fraying on the sidewall are serious. If you can see or feel any separation, don't ride on it.

sections.content: Rear tires wear significantly faster than front tires — often twice as fast. When your rear is worn out, consider swapping the front to the rear and fitting a fresh tire up front. You'll get more life out of both.

title: MTB Tire Types: Rubber Compounds and What They Mean
description: Soft, hard, dual compound — understanding rubber compounds will help you choose the right tire for your riding and conditions.

sections.content: Walk into any bike shop and you'll find MTB tires with names like Soft Compound, Dual Compound, MaxGrip, or TrailShield. It can feel like marketing noise — but there's real substance behind the terminology. Understanding rubber compounds will help you choose the right tire for your riding and conditions.

sections.heading: What is a tire compound?
sections.content: The rubber used in a tire isn't just rubber — it's a carefully engineered blend of natural rubber, synthetic polymers, carbon black, and chemical additives. The specific recipe determines how soft or hard the rubber is, measured on a durometer scale. Softer rubber grips better. Harder rubber lasts longer. Everything in tire design is a tradeoff between these two things.

sections.heading: Hard compound tires
sections.content: Hard compounds use a denser, stiffer rubber that resists wear. Grip is lower with less surface contact and conformity to terrain. Rolling resistance is lower — rolls faster on smooth surfaces. Durability is high with a significantly longer lifespan. Best for: cross-country racing, hardpack trails, dry conditions where speed matters more than grip.

sections.heading: Soft compound tires
sections.content: Soft compounds use a more pliable rubber that deforms to wrap around rocks, roots, and loose terrain. Grip is high with excellent traction in technical or loose conditions. Rolling resistance is higher with more drag especially on smooth surfaces. Durability is lower — wears faster on abrasive surfaces. Best for: enduro, gravity, wet conditions, technical terrain.

sections.heading: Dual compound tires
sections.content: Most quality MTB tires today use dual compounds — a harder rubber in the center of the tread for rolling efficiency, and softer rubber on the side knobs for cornering grip. Best for: trail riding and all-mountain — the best balance for most riders.

sections.heading: Casing matters too
sections.content: Compound is only part of the story. The casing — the woven fabric beneath the rubber — affects weight, puncture resistance, and how the tire conforms to terrain. Light casings (60–120tpi) are lighter and more supple but less puncture resistant. Heavy or reinforced casings (EXO, DH casing) are heavier but much more resistant to cuts and sidewall tears. Dual-ply uses two layers for maximum protection — used in downhill and aggressive enduro.

Many riders run a softer compound up front for maximum grip and braking traction, and a harder or dual compound on the rear where rolling efficiency and durability matter more. Front and rear tires don't need to match.

title: Choosing the Right Road Tire
description: Width, compound, casing, and construction — here's what actually matters when choosing a road tire.

sections.content: Road tires look simple compared to their knobby MTB cousins, but the choices you make — width, compound, casing, and construction — have a huge impact on speed, comfort, and puncture resistance. Here's what actually matters.

sections.heading: Width: bigger is faster (within reason)
sections.content: The old assumption was that narrower tires were faster. Research has flipped that on its head. A wider tire at lower pressure deforms around road imperfections rather than bouncing off them, reducing energy loss. Most road riders have moved to 28–32mm as the sweet spot. 23–25mm: still used in racing on smooth circuits, very fast on perfect pavement but harsh everywhere else. 28–30mm: the current road sweet spot — fast, comfortable, good puncture resistance. 32–35mm: borders on gravel territory, excellent comfort and versatility with slightly more rolling resistance.

sections.heading: Clincher vs Tubeless vs Tubular
sections.content: Clincher (with tube): the classic setup — easy to repair, widely compatible, affordable, still a great choice for most riders. Tubeless: no inner tube, sealant plugs small punctures automatically, lower rolling resistance, can run slightly lower pressure, more setup complexity but increasingly popular. Tubular: the tire and tube are one unit glued to the rim, used almost exclusively in professional racing and not practical for most riders.

sections.heading: Compound and casing
sections.content: Hard compound center with soft compound edges is common on dual-compound tires — efficient rolling straight ahead with good grip in corners. TPI (threads per inch): higher TPI means a more supple casing with better ride feel and lower rolling resistance — 120TPI and above is considered high quality. Folding vs wire bead: folding bead tires use kevlar instead of steel wire — lighter and easier to carry as a spare.

sections.heading: Puncture protection
sections.content: Most road tires include a puncture protection layer — a belt of kevlar or similar material beneath the tread. More protection adds weight and slightly increases rolling resistance. Minimal protection: race tires — light, fast, but vulnerable. Standard protection: the everyday choice — good balance. Maximum protection: commuter/training tires — heavier but durable.
Don't cheap out on tires. They're the only contact point between you and the road — a quality tire improves ride feel, speed, and safety more than almost any other upgrade at the same price point.
